setting: Leiden University Medical Center, tertiary neonatal centre
design: retrospective follow-up cohort with matched controls

intervention: neonatal hyperglycaemia (blood glucose >=10 mmol/L) treated with insulin for >=12 hours
outcomes_measured: growth (weight/length/head circumference) and neurological/behavioural development at 2 years corrected age
primary_result: growth was similar between groups; neurological and behavioural development were more frequently abnormal in the hyperglycaemia group
effect_size: neurological development abnormal more frequently in hyperglycaemia group; behavioural development abnormal more frequently in hyperglycaemia group
secondary_results: mortality substantially higher in hyperglycaemia group during admission (41% vs 8%, p<0.001), especially in <=1000g or 24-28 week infants

rob_tool: not applied (retrospective cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)

directness: DIRECT - very preterm <=32 weeks, insulin-treated hyperglycaemia population
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, small matched-control comparison, high mortality in exposed group raising survivor-bias concern); imprecision (n=33 exposed survivors)
key_limitation: one of the few studies with a clear insulin-treated preterm hyperglycaemia population and 2-year neurodevelopmental/behavioural outcome; high in-hospital mortality (41%) in the hyperglycaemia group is itself a major finding, separate from the survivor neurodevelopmental signal
notes: PMC2915976 (open access); mortality difference is a critical companion finding to the neurodevelopmental signal in survivors
glucose_threshold_used: >=10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) treated with insulin >=12 hours
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (clinical blood glucose monitoring)

population_detail: very-low-birth-weight infants (birth weight <1500g), days 1-7 of life
intervention: continuous insulin infusion 0.05 U/kg/h with 20% dextrose support (days 1-7)
outcomes_measured: mortality at expected date of delivery (primary); hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia rates; growth; morbidity
primary_result: no difference in intention-to-treat primary outcome (mortality at EDD) or secondary morbidity; early insulin reduced hyperglycaemia but increased hypoglycaemia; mortality at 28 days was HIGHER in early-insulin group
effect_size: mean glucose 6.2 vs 6.7 mmol/L; hyperglycaemia >10% of week1 in 21% vs 33%; hypoglycaemia (<2.6mmol/L >1h) 29% vs 17%; 28-day mortality higher in insulin group
secondary_results: trial STOPPED EARLY for futility on primary outcome and concern about potential harm; early-insulin group had more carbohydrate infused and less weight loss in week 1 (both statistically significant) - the only clearly favourable secondary signals
ascertainment_method: continuous glucose monitoring used to assess efficacy of glucose control; trial registered ISRCTN78428828
rob_tool: not applied (RCT; early stopping and harm signal noted directly in abstract)
rob_overall: Low (adequately randomised and multicentre, but stopped early with a mortality signal - genuine risk of bias from early stopping plus imprecision from reduced sample)
directness: DIRECT - VLBW/preterm infants - the key interventional (insulin) trial for this population; NO published long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of this cohort was located this session (see search log)
grade_reason: risk of bias (trial stopped early for futility/harm - a classic source of overestimated harm and underestimated benefit); imprecision (reduced sample from early stopping)
key_limitation: THIS IS THE TRIAL THE RESEARCH BRIEF REFERS TO AS THE 'COIN TRIAL' - no trial by that name exists in the literature (confirmed by targeted search); NIRTURE is the correct identifier. Early insulin REDUCES hyperglycaemia but at the cost of MORE hypoglycaemia and a signal toward HIGHER 28-day mortality - a genuine harm signal, reported with full prominence, not softened. No neurodevelopmental follow-up of this RCT cohort has been published to date - a real evidence gap, not an extrapolation.
notes: Trial stopped early for futility/harm concerns; ISRCTN78428828; this is the single most important interventional trial in this domain and the clearest example of a null/harmful finding given equal prominence to positive findings elsewhere in the domain
glucose_threshold_used: treatment threshold not a single value - insulin titrated to target euglycaemia; hyperglycaemia defined as blood glucose above normal range per protocol
glucose_measurement_method: continuous glucose monitoring used for efficacy assessment; standard glucometer for clinical management
outcome_timepoint: 28 days (mortality only) - NO neurodevelopmental follow-up published
dose_response_reported: N (single intervention arm comparison; no dose-response reported)

n_events: 4 glycaemic groups: normoglycaemic, hypoglycaemic, hyperglycaemic, unstable
population_detail: very preterm infants, birth weight <1500g or gestation <30 weeks, admitted within 24h to a single NZ tertiary unit
intervention: n/a (observational glycaemic-group exposure based on first-week glucose profile)
outcomes_measured: survival without neonatal morbidity; survival without neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years; glucose variability (SD of log-transformed glucose) as a separate predictor
primary_result: hyperglycaemic and unstable groups less likely to survive without morbidity or without neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years IN UNADJUSTED ANALYSIS; NO associations survived adjustment for gestation/birth-weight z-score/socioeconomic status
effect_size: higher mean glucose associated with worse neonatal and 2-year outcomes (unadjusted); greater glucose variability associated with worse neonatal illness but NOT with 2-year outcome
p_value: not reported as single value (multivariable regression reported as non-significant after adjustment)
secondary_results: hypoglycaemic infants had outcomes similar to normoglycaemic infants (null); glucose variability specifically was NOT an independent predictor of 2-year outcome once gestation/birth-weight/SES were accounted for - directly addresses the glycaemic-lability-for-hyperglycaemia question with a NULL result after adjustment
ascertainment_method: retrospective glucose concentration records from first week of life; standardised 2-year neurodevelopmental assessment
rob_tool: not applied (retrospective cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate (retrospective, single-centre, but multivariable adjustment for key confounders explicitly performed and changes the headline result)
directness: DIRECT - very preterm <30 weeks/<1500g
grade_reason: indirectness/confounding (key finding is that unadjusted glycaemic-group associations do not survive adjustment for gestation and growth - i.e. glycaemia is likely a MARKER of immaturity/growth restriction rather than an independent causal exposure); single-centre imprecision
key_limitation: CENTRAL paper for the glycaemic-variability-in-hyperglycaemia question posed by the task: variability (MAGE/SD-based) was associated with worse NEONATAL illness but NOT independently with 2-year outcome after adjustment - this is a genuine null for variability-as-independent-predictor and should not be overstated as confirming lability's importance
notes: Auckland/Liggins-programme-adjacent (Harding senior author) but methodologically distinct from CHYLD - a retrospective glycaemic-profile cohort, not a treat-to-threshold RCT

glucose_threshold_used: exposure defined by profile group, not single threshold; hyperglycaemic/unstable groups defined by absolute glycaemic excursions in first week
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (retrospective clinical glucose records)

population_detail: preterm infants randomised within 6 hours of life
intervention: real-time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-guided glycaemic management
comparator: blinded CGM with standard intermittent blood glucose-guided management

effect_size: hyperglycaemia episodes first week 145 vs 830; hypoglycaemia episodes first week 339 vs 934; hyperglycaemia at 32 weeks PMA 1 vs 38
secondary_results: reduction in glycaemic excursions did not translate into a detectable neurodevelopmental benefit at 2 years - reported as a null result with equal prominence to the positive glycaemic-control finding

notes: Very recent (2026); small trial, likely underpowered for the neurodevelopmental outcome despite being adequately powered for the glycaemic-control primary outcome - flag this distinction clearly

glucose_measurement_method: continuous glucose monitoring (intervention arm) vs intermittent blood glucose (control arm)

grade_reason: imprecision (n=53, self-evidently underpowered for ND outcome); should be read as hypothesis-generating, not evidence of safety-equivalence
key_limitation: the only preterm CGM RCT with a 2-year ND readout, and it is null but underpowered
notes: cross-referenced in both Domain D (preterm variability) and Domain G (hyperglycaemia variability) - same trial relevant to both questions
glucose_threshold_used: not a single threshold - variability/episode-count outcome

design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (current edition, pub3, supersedes pub2/2020)
population_detail: preterm infants at risk of hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia
outcomes_measured: neurodevelopmental impairment (primary outcome); seizures; in-hospital mortality
primary_result: NONE of the 4 included trials reported neurodevelopmental impairment, nor did any report seizures; effect on mortality uncertain
effect_size: RR 0.59 (in-hospital mortality)
secondary_results: 'insufficient evidence to determine if CGM affects preterm infant mortality or morbidities'; certainty very low across all outcomes
rob_overall: very low certainty across all outcomes (risk of bias, imprecision)
directness: direct - preterm population, but the review's OWN primary outcome (neurodevelopmental impairment) was unreported by every included trial
grade_reason: risk of bias; imprecision; the central negative finding is that the primary outcome was simply not measured by any pooled trial
key_limitation: no studies identified in preterm infants with PROVEN (rather than at-risk-of) hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia
notes: Cochrane-level, independent confirmation that the preterm CGM literature has not yet closed the gap to long-term outcome evidence - corroborates this domain's central evidence-gap finding
glucose_threshold_used: not applicable (review of monitoring modality)
glucose_measurement_method: continuous glucose monitoring vs standard intermittent
outcome_timepoint: in-hospital (mortality); ND outcome not reported by any trial
dose_response_reported: not reported by any included trial (review's own central negative finding)

population_detail: hypoglycaemic neonates
outcomes_measured: MRI abnormality vs glucose nadir, duration/recurrence of hypoglycaemia, seizure occurrence
primary_result: days of hypoglycaemia (not lowest glucose value) significantly associated with abnormal MRI; lowest glucose significantly lower in infants who had seizures
p_value: <.001 (duration vs abnormal MRI); <.01 (glucose nadir vs seizures); >.05 (glucose nadir vs abnormal MRI, not significant)
directness: indirect - non-UK retrospective cohort; term/preterm mix not specified in abstract
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, single-centre, non-UK); imprecision
key_limitation: duration/recurrence, not glucose nadir, tracks with imaging abnormality - nuanced finding, glucose nadir does track with seizure occurrence specifically
notes: most common abnormal MRI site: parietal/occipital; key evidence for duration-over-severity as driver of imaging abnormality
glucose_threshold_used: not a single threshold - duration/recurrence analysis
dose_response_reported: Y (duration/recurrence, not absolute severity, associated with abnormal MRI)

population_detail: neonates with hypoglycaemic brain injury, serial imaging
outcomes_measured: MRI evolution (DWI to T1/T2); glucose nadir vs injury extent
primary_result: occipital/parietal cortex most vulnerable; DWI hyperintensity earliest detectable sign; minimum glucose significantly lower in infants with widespread cortical injury vs occipital-parietal-only injury
effect_size: minimum glucose 0.71+/-0.35 vs 1.19+/-0.42 mmol/L (widespread vs focal injury)
directness: indirect - non-UK, small case series, Chinese language full text
grade_reason: imprecision (n=16); risk of bias (small case series); inconsistency (sits in tension with Gu 2019's larger duration-over-severity finding)
key_limitation: [abstract only] - Chinese language, English abstract only, full text not accessed
notes: in this small series, glucose nadir DID track with extent of injury - tension with Gu 2019's finding that duration (not nadir) predicts abnormal MRI; both reported, not adjudicated
outcome_timepoint: serial imaging (timing not specified beyond serial)
dose_response_reported: Y (glucose nadir associated with injury extent in this series)

n_patients: 11 children with seizures beyond infancy after neonatal hypoglycaemia (perinatal asphyxia excluded)
outcomes_measured: MRI findings; later epilepsy phenotype
primary_result: all 11 had MRI evidence of occipital +/- parietal gliosis/atrophy; seizure phenotype genuinely variable
secondary_results: focal occipital seizures in 9 (infrequent/remitted in 6 of these); generalised tonic seizures in 2 (frequent, refractory)
directness: indirect - non-UK, small referral-clinic case series
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, referral-selected); imprecision (n=11); consistent direction across other independent cohorts (Kapoor, Yalcin) increases confidence in the qualitative pattern
key_limitation: genuine null-to-mixed result on whether injury pattern alone predicts epilepsy severity
notes: mean age at seizure onset 10.3 months; clinic follow-up to time of study
outcome_timepoint: mean age at seizure onset 10.3 months; clinic follow-up to time of study

n_patients: 170 children with epilepsy secondary to documented neonatal hypoglycaemic brain injury (10-year period)
outcomes_measured: MRI pattern; seizure type; comorbidity (developmental delay, cerebral palsy, vision impairment, microcephaly)
primary_result: MRI showed occipital +/- parietal gliosis/encephalomalacia in 96.5%; epileptic spasms dominant seizure type (76.5%); 68.2% drug-resistant epilepsy
secondary_results: global developmental delay 91.2%; cerebral palsy 48.7%; vision impairment 48.2%; microcephaly 38.2%
rob_overall: high (LMIC referral-clinic population, established/often refractory epilepsy, severe end of spectrum)
directness: indirect - explicitly a low-resource LMIC setting; very high comorbidity rates should not be read as representative of UK-expected outcomes with earlier detection/treatment
grade_certainty: Low-Moderate (for the qualitative injury-pattern-to-epilepsy link, consistent with 3 other independent cohorts)
grade_reason: risk of bias (referral/clinic-selected, retrospective); indirectness (LMIC low-resource setting, severe end of spectrum)
key_limitation: largest case series in this domain by a wide margin (n=170), but least UK-generalisable given resource/detection-timing differences
notes: PMID initially flagged as unresolvable in scoping (batch-call artefact) - resolved cleanly this session via solo metadata call and independent title search; valid, verifiable citation

n_patients: 45 neonates (term and preterm) with DWI after hypoglycaemia; 25 scanned within 6 days
outcomes_measured: DWI timing sensitivity for occipital diffusion restriction, by gestation and scan timing
primary_result: occipital diffusion restriction seen in 8/16 (50%) TERM infants scanned within 6 days, but ZERO preterm infants; among 20 infants scanned beyond 6 days, no occipital diffusion restriction seen at all even where hypoglycaemia ongoing
secondary_results: diffusion restriction correlated with abnormal visual evoked potentials and later cortical visual deficit
rob_overall: moderate (retrospective, non-UK, single-centre, likely non-protocolised scan timing)
directness: direct for term infants; the preterm-negative finding is a directness-limiting caution against extrapolation, not proof of absence of preterm injury (small preterm subgroup)
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, non-UK, single-centre); imprecision (small samples within the sensitive window); consistency is a strength (concordant with Zhang 2022, 14 years later, different country)
key_limitation: DWI sensitivity established in term infants does NOT extend to preterm infants in this dataset (very serious imprecision in the small preterm subgroup)
notes: foundational pre-2015 paper retained per brief's rule; central evidence for the MRI-timing recommendation (scan within ~1 week)
glucose_measurement_method: whole blood glucose (not specified point-of-care vs lab)
outcome_timepoint: scan within 6 days vs beyond 6 days of hypoglycaemia onset
dose_response_reported: Y (scan timing relative to onset determined sensitivity; term vs preterm gestation also modified sensitivity)

outcomes_measured: DWI/T1/T2 evolution over time; vulnerable injury sites; extensive vs focal injury and clinical severity
primary_result: 84 scans showed injury-site DWI hyperintensity within 7 days; 39 scans showed evolution to abnormal T1/T2 at 11-23 days; repeat scans in 13 infants at 9-20 days showed NO abnormal signal at all
secondary_results: vulnerable sites: occipital lobe 98%, splenium of corpus callosum 60%, parietal lobe 30%; extensive injury (n=20) had significantly higher rates of recurrent convulsions, respiratory failure, coma, death/severe NDI than focal injury (n=66) - authors note extensive pattern may partly reflect coexisting hypoxia-ischaemia
directness: indirect - non-UK single-centre retrospective series
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, non-UK); imprecision; consistency with Tam 2008 (14 years apart, different country, concordant DWI-timing pattern) increases confidence in the qualitative timing pattern
key_limitation: most direct 2015+ MRI-timing paper found; extensive-injury cases may reflect coexisting HIE rather than hypoglycaemia in isolation - relevant to differential-diagnosis point
notes: together with Tam 2008, forms the empirical basis for the 'scan within the first week' recommendation
outcome_timepoint: DWI within 7 days; T1/T2 evolution at 11-23 days; repeat scans 9-20 days
dose_response_reported: Y (extensive vs focal injury tracked clinical severity and outcome)

outcomes_measured: MRI occipital injury; flash visual evoked potentials (FVEP); timing of hypoglycaemia detection vs seizure occurrence
primary_result: 80% of hypoglycaemia group had occipital-lobe injury on MRI; FVEP 100% sensitive but only 25% specific for parieto-occipital injury (cannot substitute for MRI)
secondary_results: infants who went on to have seizures detected as hypoglycaemic LATER (median 51h) than those who did not (median 22h)
directness: indirect - non-UK, small case-control study
grade_reason: risk of bias (small case-control, non-UK); imprecision (n=15 vs 11)
key_limitation: suggests delayed recognition, not simply glucose depth, contributes to the seizure phenotype
notes: FVEP cannot substitute for MRI despite high sensitivity, due to poor specificity

population_detail: all neonates, all gestations per guideline scope
outcomes_measured: clinical indications and optimal MRI timing across neonatal pathologies including hypoglycaemia-associated brain damage
primary_result: names hypoglycaemia-associated brain damage as a condition with its own MRI timing considerations; specific timing value not extractable without full text
directness: not an interventional/primary evidence claim - labelled as GUIDANCE, not folded into peer-reviewed evidence count per project non-negotiable rule
grade_reason: n/a
key_limitation: [abstract only] - no PMC full text available (confirmed via convert_article_ids); exact timing recommendation for hypoglycaemia specifically not extractable without full text; first author's affiliation (Hammersmith Hospital/Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust) is the SAME TRUST as this synthesis and as Burns 2008
notes: MOST RECENT (2025) and only guideline-tier source found addressing MRI timing for hypoglycaemia-associated brain damage specifically; not UK/BAPM-authored (Spanish Neonatal Brain Group) but first author is Hammersmith/ICHNT-affiliated - priority follow-up to obtain in full text

n_patients: 21 with documented hypoglycaemia and typical parieto-occipital injury
outcomes_measured: epilepsy; refractoriness; cerebral palsy; VEP abnormality; injury topography vs prolonged hypoglycaemia
primary_result: 85.7% developed epilepsy, 38.1% refractory, 33.3% cerebral palsy, 100% of tested (18/18) had abnormal VEP
secondary_results: prolonged hypoglycaemia (recurrent episodes >12h) associated with significantly greater parieto-occipital involvement and spasticity
directness: indirect - non-UK, third independent cohort (after Fong 2014, Kapoor 2020) cross-validating the injury-pattern-to-epilepsy/CP/visual-impairment linkage
grade_certainty: Low-Moderate (consistent direction across independent cohorts strengthens qualitative confidence)
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, referral-selected); indirectness (non-UK)
key_limitation: strengthens confidence in phenotype description even though no underlying cohort is UK-based or population-representative
notes: prolonged/recurrent (not single-episode) hypoglycaemia predicted more severe topography and outcome, consistent with the recurrence-over-severity pattern seen elsewhere in this review
outcome_timepoint: retrospective clinic follow-up, ages/duration not uniformly specified
dose_response_reported: Y (prolonged vs non-prolonged hypoglycaemia predicted parieto-occipital involvement/spasticity)

outcomes_measured: long-term deficit phenotype from parieto-temporo-occipital injury
primary_result: demonstrates a non-visual long-term deficit (slowed reading, impaired phonological awareness) without cortical blindness or visual field defect
directness: indirect - single case report, non-UK
grade_reason: single case report; not generalisable
key_limitation: useful reminder that the outcome phenotype extends beyond commonly emphasised cortical visual impairment
notes: illustrative case, not primary evidence for prevalence/rate claims
